content: The World Health Organization (WHO) excluded certain medicines previously recommended in the past (n=346). When drug susceptibility testing (DST) results were available, a medicine was deemed effective if the results indicated susceptibility and ineffective if resistance was observed. In cases where DST results were missing, two scenarios were considered. First, if the prevalence of resistance to a medicine was less than 10% in the same population (either from the same country or study site, or overall if local data were unavailable), the medicine was considered effective. This applied to agents such as cycloserine or terizidone, linezolid, clofazimine, bedaquiline, carbapenems, and delamanid. Second, if the prevalence of resistance was 10% or higher, imputed DST results were used to determine effectiveness. If the imputed DST result showed susceptibility, the medicine was counted as effective; if resistance was shown, it was not. This applied to agents like pyrazinamide, ethambutol, second-line injectable agents, fluoroquinolones, p-aminosalicylic acid, ethionamide, and prothionamide. Certain agents were excluded from the count of medicines likely to be effective, regardless of DST results. These included isoniazid (including high-dose isoniazid), rifampicin, rifabutin, thioacetazone, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and macrolide antibiotics. Subsets of the 2018 individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis, which included 13,104 patients from 53 studies across 40 countries, were analyzed to assess the risk of treatment failure, relapse, and success associated with different treatment durations. Patients were followed up for relapse, but the number of reported relapse cases was relatively small. For PICO question 5 (2018), which examined different durations of the intensive phase of treatment for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB), the primary analysis included data from 3,750 patients across 42 observational studies. Of these, 2,720 received individualized MDR-TB regimens, and 1,030 received standardized regimens. From the main IPD dataset, 9,354 records were excluded for reasons such as loss to follow-up (n=2,261), death (n=2,043), lack of injectable use (n=1,094), missing information on injectable duration (n=2,341), fewer than five effective medicines or fewer than four plus pyrazinamide (n=1,450), and injectable duration longer than 20 months (n=165). For PICO question 6 (2018), which focused on regimen duration, the primary analysis included 6,356 patients from 51 observational studies. Of these, 5,352 received individualized MDR-TB regimens, and 1,004 received standardized regimens. From the main IPD dataset, 6,748 records were excluded for reasons such as loss to follow-up (n=2,261), death (n=2,043), missing treatment duration (n=230), fewer than five effective drugs or fewer than four plus pyrazinamide (n=2,072), treatment duration less than six months (n=52), and treatment duration of 36 months or more (n=90). For PICO question 7 (2018), which examined treatment duration after culture conversion, the analysis included 4,175 patients from 39 observational studies, with all but three on individualized regimens. A total of 8,929 records were excluded for reasons such as loss to follow-up (n=2,261), death (n=2,043), missing treatment duration (n=230), missing culture information (n=1,945), baseline culture-negative status (n=754), no culture conversion (n=426), fewer than five effective drugs or fewer than four plus pyrazinamide (n=1,215), treatment duration less than six months (n=4), treatment duration of 36 months or more (n=49), and post-treatment culture conversion (n=2). Ultimately, 515 patients met the criteria, with 242 receiving bedaquiline for more than 203 days and 273 receiving it for 168–203 days. Additional data sources considered by the 2019 Guideline Development Group (GDG) included cohorts from Belarus (112 patients) and Uzbekistan (123 patients), with 65 and 72 patients, respectively, receiving bedaquiline for more than 203 days or 168–203 days. The primary analyses focused on data from the endTB observational study. For PICO question 2 (2019), which examined the concurrent use of bedaquiline and delamanid, data were derived from the same endTB cohort. However, only 92 patients received both medicines together, with even fewer starting both within the first month of treatment (n=35). An additional three patients received both medicines by the end of the first month, bringing the total to 38. The remaining 57 patients started the medicines more than 30 days apart and were excluded. Additional data sources included a cohort of 100 patients treated with bedaquiline in Mumbai, India, of whom 86 received some form of concomitant treatment with bedaquiline and delamanid. Of these, 62 initiated the medicines within 30 days of each other, and 46 began both during the first month of treatment. The total intervention population comprised 84 patients: 38 from the endTB cohort and 46 from the Mumbai dataset. The comparator group included 401 patients who initiated bedaquiline within the first month of treatment and did not receive it beyond six months. A secondary comparator group included 102 patients who received delamanid within the first month of treatment without extended use. The DELIBERATE trial, a randomized, open-label, three-arm pharmacokinetic and safety trial conducted in Peru and South Africa, provided additional safety data. Eligible patients were adults with pulmonary MDR-TB or rifampicin-monoresistant TB receiving treatment without clofazimine and with levofloxacin replacing moxifloxacin. The trial compared QTcF changes when bedaquiline and delamanid were co-administered versus when each drug was administered alone. Preliminary data from the trial were made available in July 2019, with low certainty in the estimates of effect. For PICO question 1 (2021), which examined the use of bedaquiline in children under six years old, data from two Phase 2 trials (TMC207-C211 and IMPAACT P1108) were reviewed. The review focused on pharmacokinetics and safety data from IMPAACT P1108, which included children aged 0–6 years. Although the sample size was small (n=12), the GDG concluded that cardiac safety signals in children aged 0–6 years were not distinct from those in adults. Population pharmacokinetic models suggested that drug exposures observed in adults could be achieved in most children, though dose modifications might be necessary based on age and weight. A pediatric MDR/RR-TB IPD analysis included 24,231 records, with just under 20,000 used for a matched analysis of treatment outcomes in children. The analysis included 40 children under six years old and 68 children aged 6–12 years who received bedaquiline. Bedaquiline was associated with shorter treatment duration and reduced use of injectable TB drugs. A child-friendly 20 mg formulation of bedaquiline is being used in ongoing studies, with indirect bioequivalence testing showing similar bioavailability to the 100 mg formulation. Findings from the bedaquiline crush study indicated that suspending the tablets in water did not affect bioavailability.
